finalText:
**Merge** combines two branches by creating a commit that ties them together. Your history shows both branches, and you can see exactly when the merge happened. It's nondestructive — nothing gets rewritten.

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of another branch, rewriting history so it looks like you always built on the latest. No merge commit, just a linear history.

**Key differences:**

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Shows the merge point; two parents visible | Linear; looks like one continuous flow |
| Reversible | Yes, just revert the merge commit | No (rewrites history) |
| Conflicts | One merge-conflict resolution | Conflicts on each replayed commit |
| Collaboration | Safe on shared/public branches | Risky if others have fetched your branch |

**When to use each:**

- **Merge**: On shared branches (main, release branches) or when working with others on the same branch. The "truth" of when work integrated matters.
- **Rebase**: On feature branches before merging to main — cleans up your commits and makes PR review easier. Use it locally while your branch is only yours.

**Practical rule of thumb:** Rebase locally to keep your feature branch tidy, then merge to main. Don't rebase after you've pushed (others may have built on your commits). Never force-push a shared branch.

The safety concern is real: if you rebase and force-push a branch that someone else is working on, they'll have a bad time merging your "new" commits with their work. Merge is always the safer choice on shared work.
